verdict.rationale: Paul's chain of past-tense verbs (aorist, a completed past action) in Romans 8:30 closes with 'he glorified' (edoxasen), placing glorification as the terminal link of the salvific sequence, stated in the same completed past tense of certainty as the prior verbs 'he predestined' (proorisen), 'he called' (ekalesen), and 'he justified' (edikaiosen). First Corinthians 15:42 to 57 builds a sustained antithetical lexical field: 'corruption' (phthora) versus 'incorruption' (aphtharsia), 'dishonor' (atimia) versus 'glory' (doxa), 'weakness' (astheneia) versus 'power' (dunamis), 'soulish' (psychikon) versus 'spiritual' (pneumatikon), and 'mortal' (thnetos) versus 'immortality' (athanasia), with the verbs 'it is raised' (egeiretai), 'we shall be changed' (allagesometha), and 'to put on' (endusasthai) naming the resurrection transformation while the noun 'body' (soma) is retained throughout. Philippians 3:21 caps it with 'he will refashion the body' (metaschematisei to soma) and 'conformed to the body of his glory' (symmorphon to somati tes doxes autou), and First John 3:2 with 'we shall be like him' (homoioi auto esometha) anchored to seeing him as he is. Romans 8:18 to 23 extends the hope to creation under 'corruption' (phthora) awaiting 'the freedom of the glory' (eleutherias tes doxes) and 'the redemption of the body' (apolytrosin tou somatos). The pattern is dense and spread across the whole Bible (pan-canonical) within Paul's and John's writings, and is not variant-sensitive at the verdict level. The verb 'to glorify' (doxazo) applied to the believer and the term 'conformed' (symmorphos) are individually rare, so the certainty rests on the convergence of the whole field rather than on the frequency of any single term.

scripture.reasoning: The chain of completed past-tense verbs (aorist, a completed past action) 'he predestined' (proorisen), 'he called' (ekalesen), 'he justified' (edikaiosen), and 'he glorified' (edoxasen) places 'he glorified' (edoxasen) as the terminal anticipatory (proleptic, spoken of in advance as already settled) act of the order of salvation, stated in the same completed past tense as the prior links so that the future glory is spoken of as already certain. Of the 62 canon uses of 'to glorify' (doxazo), the believer is the object of final glorification in only a handful, chiefly here and Romans 8:17, so the term is decisive here but not frequent.

'He predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son' (proorisen symmorphous tes eikonos tou huiou autou). The believer is predestined to be conformed to the image of the Son. This is one of only two canon uses of 'conformed' (symmorphos), and it sets up the same conformity that Philippians 3:21 will give to the resurrection body, making the verdict-bearing conformity language spread across all of Paul (pan-Pauline) rather than isolated.

The antithetical pairing 'it is sown in corruption, it is raised in incorruption' (speiretai en phthora, egeiretai en aphtharsia) binds resurrection to incorruption, with present passive verbs (ongoing action done to the subject) marking divine agency.

'It is sown in dishonor, it is raised in glory' (speiretai en atimia, egeiretai en doxe) and 'it is sown in weakness, it is raised in power' (speiretai en astheneia, egeiretai en dunamei) extend the antithetical column, naming 'glory' (doxa) as the state into which the body is raised.

'A soulish body' (soma psychikon) versus 'a spiritual body' (soma pneumatikon). The retained noun 'body' (soma) rules out disembodied survival, while the adjectives mark the qualitative transformation of the same body. 'Soulish' (psychikos) is rare, only 6 uses, but its contrast partner 'spiritual' (pneumatikos) and the kept noun 'body' (soma) fix the sense as animated-by-soul versus animated-by-Spirit.

First-Adam, last-Adam pattern (typology, an Old Testament person prefiguring a New Testament reality): 'the first man Adam became a living soul, the last Adam a life-giving spirit' (ho protos anthropos Adam eis psychen zosan, ho eschatos Adam eis pneuma zoopoioun). The last Adam is the source of the life-giving spirit that powers the resurrected body.

'The first man from the earth, earthy; the second man from heaven' (ho protos anthropos ek ges choikos, ho deuteros anthropos ex ouranou). The earthy versus heavenly polarity grounds the two-body classification (taxonomy, an ordered classification) in two representative humans. 'Earthy, made of dust' (choikos) occurs only 4 times, all in this paragraph, so its sense is set by this context alone.

'Just as we have borne the image of the earthy, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly' (kathos ephoresamen ten eikona tou choikou, phoresomen kai ten eikona tou epouraniou). The verb names the believer's assumption of the heavenly image, with 'image' (eikon) linking back to 'conformed to the image' (symmorphous tes eikonos) in Romans 8:29.

'Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does corruption inherit incorruption' (sarx kai haima basileian theou kleronomesai ou dynatai, oude he phthora ten aphtharsian kleronomei). The inheritance of the kingdom requires the corruption-to-incorruption transition.

'We shall all be changed' (pantes allagesometha). The future passive plural (a future action done to many subjects) locates the change as a future divine act on all who are Christ's. 'To change' (allasso) is used 6 times, twice here in verses 51 to 52 of this transformation.

'The dead will be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed' (hoi nekroi egerthesontai aphthartoi, kai hemeis allagesometha). The dead are raised incorruptible and the living are changed at the end-time (eschatological, having to do with the last things) trumpet.

'For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality' (dei gar to phtharton touto endusasthai aphtharsian kai to thneton touto endusasthai athanasian). The clothing image names what must be put on, with 'it is necessary' (dei) marking divine necessity. 'Immortality' (athanasia) occurs only 3 times, but the paired 'incorruption' (aphtharsia) and the verb 'to put on' (endusasthai) fix the sense.
'Death has been swallowed up into victory' (katepothe ho thanatos eis nikos) quotes Isaiah 25:8. Death is swallowed up into victory at the donning of incorruption.

'Who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ' (to didonti hemin to nikos dia tou kyriou hemon Iesou Christou). The victory over death is given through Christ, securing the resurrection outcome.

'He will refashion the body of our lowliness conformed to the body of his glory' (metaschematisei to soma tes tapeinoseos hemon symmorphon to somati tes doxes autou). The verb 'to change in fashion' (metaschematizo) takes 'body' (soma) as its object, and 'conformed' (symmorphos), used with the 'to-form' grammatical case (dative), names the result. 'Conformed' (symmorphos) occurs only here and Romans 8:29, so its two uses both point to conformity to Christ, making the sense stable despite the rarity.

'We shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is' (homoioi auto esometha, hoti opsometha auton kathos estin). The future state is likeness to the appearing Christ, with sight of him as he is as the formative cause. The word is 'like or resembling' (homoios), the adjective, with 46 canon uses, not the verbal 'to make like' (homoioo) of the parable formulas, so the claim is qualitative likeness to Christ.

'The sufferings of this present time are not worthy compared with the coming glory to be revealed in us' (ouk axia ta pathemata tou nyn kairou pros ten mellousan doxan apokalyphthenai eis hemas). Present suffering is set against a coming 'glory' (doxa) yet to be revealed into us.

'The creation itself will be set free from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God' (he ktisis eleutherothesetai apo tes douleias tes phthoras eis ten eleutherian tes doxes ton teknon tou theou). 'Creation' (ktisis) itself is brought into the glory-freedom of the children of God.

'Awaiting adoption, the redemption of our body' (apekdechomenoi huiothesian, ten apolytrosin tou somatos hemon). The hoped-for adoption is identified with the redemption of the 'body' (soma), naming bodily resurrection as the content of glorification.

'When Christ is manifested, then you also will be manifested with him in glory' (hotan ho Christos phanerothe, tote kai hymeis syn auto phanerothesesthe en doxe). When Christ is manifested, the believers are manifested with him in 'glory' (doxa). The cross-reference network ties this directly to First John 3:2 and Philippians 3:21, repeating the appearing-then-glory sequence.

complicating_texts.resolution: 'Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God' (sarx kai haima basileian theou kleronomesai ou dynatai) is sometimes read as denying bodily resurrection. The immediate context resolves this. Paul uses 'flesh and blood' (sarx kai haima) as a fixed idiom for mortal corruptible existence, paralleled by 'the corruption' (he phthora) in the same verse, then immediately predicts 'we shall be changed' (allagesometha) and 'to put on incorruption' (endusasthai aphtharsian), confirming continuity of 'body' (soma) with transformation of mode rather than abolition of the body.

'We shall not all sleep' (pantes ou koimethesometha) versus 'but we shall all be changed' (pantes de allagesometha) generates a textual variant cluster, but the verdict-bearing claim that all believers will be transformed at Christ's return holds across every plausible reading of the sleep-clause, since 'we shall be changed' (allagesometha) is undisputed in all witnesses.

The completed past-tense (aorist) 'he glorified' (edoxasen) could be read as describing a past completed glorification rather than a future one, which would seem to argue against a still-future consummation. The construction resolves this. The verb stands in a chain of four completed past-tense verbs describing the whole order of salvation as one settled divine plan, and the same letter at verses 18 to 23 places the 'glory' (doxa) as 'about to be revealed' (mellousan), and ties it to the still-awaited 'redemption of the body' (apolytrosin tou somatos), so the completed past tense is anticipatory (proleptic) certainty, not past completion.

variant_units_examined.note: Future indicative 'we shall bear' (phoresomen) versus completed past-tense subjunctive 'phoresomen' meaning the hortatory 'let us bear' is debated in the witnesses, but either reading still entails the believer's assumption of the heavenly image, so the verdict is not affected.

Word-order variants around 'not all shall sleep' (ou pantes koimethesometha) versus 'all shall not sleep' (pantes ou koimethesometha) affect the scope of who sleeps but not the universal 'we shall all be changed' (allagesometha) clause that carries the doctrinal weight.

Some witnesses omit one of the two parallel 'when' (hotan) clauses, 'the corruptible' (to phtharton) or 'the mortal' (to thneton), by a copying error where the scribe's eye skips between identical endings (homoeoteleuton), but the surviving clause and the Isaiah 25:8 citation 'death has been swallowed up into victory' (katepothe ho thanatos eis nikos) preserve the death-defeat outcome in every reading.

variants.note: None of the anchors fall in the published window of the genealogical text-critical method (CBGM, the Coherence-Based Genealogical Method), which covers only Third John 1:1 to 1:15. The New Testament anchors are read against the MorphGNT and SBLGNT critical text and the STEPBible apparatus (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) without CBGM-grade arbitration, so variant signal is treated as shadow.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: The noun 'body' (soma) is retained through First Corinthians 15:42 to 44 with only the modifier changing, 'soulish' (psychikon) to 'spiritual' (pneumatikon), and Philippians 3:21 makes the same 'body of our lowliness' (soma tes tapeinoseos) the object of 'to change in fashion' (metaschematizo) and the subject of 'conformed to the body of his glory' (symmorphon to somati tes doxes), so the future state is a transformed body, not a new substance.

A reading that reduces the future to disembodied immortality would have to discard the repeated noun 'body' (soma), the verbs 'it is raised' (egeiretai) and 'we shall be changed' (allagesometha), and 'the redemption of the body' (apolytrosin tou somatos) in Romans 8:23. Stated in its strongest form, it leans on 'spiritual body' (soma pneumatikon) meaning non-physical, but 'spiritual' (pneumatikos) elsewhere in the same letter modifies physical realities such as food and drink and rock in First Corinthians 10, so the adjective marks the animating power, not the absence of body.

In its strongest form this lens points to the completed past-tense (aorist) 'he glorified' (edoxasen) in Romans 8:30 as glory already accomplished. But the same passage marks the 'glory' (doxa) as 'about to be revealed' (mellousan) in verse 18, and the cluster of future-tense verbs 'we shall bear' (phoresomen), 'we shall be changed' (allagesometha), 'they will be raised' (egerthesontai), 'it will be set free' (eleutherothesetai), 'we shall see' (opsometha), 'we shall be' (esometha), and 'awaiting' (apekdechomenoi) place the consummation in the future, so the completed past tense functions as anticipatory (proleptic) certainty within a not-yet horizon.

The vocabulary fixes that believers will be glorified, bodily, conformed to Christ, but it does not by itself rank the timing details, such as the relation of the resurrection to a thousand-year (millennial) scheme or the exact ordering of the living and the dead beyond 'in an instant' (en atomo) at the last trumpet. This is where readers can legitimately diverge, but the divergence is over schedule and not over the verdict that final glorification occurs.

hermeneutics.notes: The lexical case turns on the convergence of three things: the retained noun 'body' (soma) with future-passive resurrection verbs, the antithetical outcome vocabulary 'glory' (doxa), 'incorruption' (aphtharsia), 'immortality' (athanasia) against 'corruption' (phthora), 'dishonor' (atimia), 'mortal' (thnetos), and the conformity terms 'conformed' (symmorphos) and 'like' (homoios) tied to Christ, all cross-referenced to the Old Testament death-defeat texts Isaiah 25:8 and Hosea 13:14 through direct citation in First Corinthians 15:54 to 55.

stem_audit.notes: The stem describes a future end-time (eschatological) state and its content: raised bodily, transformed, glorified, free from sin and decay, without smuggling a contested mechanism or a tradition-specific taxonomy (ordered classification). The terms map directly onto the Greek lexical field of 'glory' (doxa), 'incorruption' (aphtharsia), 'immortality' (athanasia), 'spiritual body' (soma pneumatikon), 'we shall be changed' (allagesometha), 'conformed' (symmorphos), so the verdict is derived from the words and not from the framing. Correction logged versus the prior file. The key term for First John 3:2 was retagged from G3666 (the verb 'to make like' (homoioo) of the parable formulas) to G3664 (the adjective 'like or resembling' (homoios)), which is the form actually present in the verse and confirmed to contain First John 3:2 in the concordance. The 'to glorify' (doxazo) canon count was corrected from 61 to the queried 62. 'Conformed' (symmorphos) G4832 and 'to change in fashion' (metaschematizo) G3345 were added as anchors after direct queries showed 'conformed' (symmorphos) occurs only twice, Romans 8:29 and Philippians 3:21, both conformity to Christ. No verdict change.

lay_summary: The Greek vocabulary across Paul and John supports the proposition with high consistency. Romans 8:30 ends a chain of four matching past-tense verbs with 'he glorified' (edoxasen), so the final glory is spoken of as already settled, even though the same chapter at verse 18 calls that glory still about to be revealed. First Corinthians 15:42 to 57 builds a sustained set of opposites. The body is sown in 'corruption' (phthora) and raised in 'incorruption' (aphtharsia). It is sown in dishonor and raised in 'glory' (doxa). It is sown in weakness and raised in power. It is sown a soulish body and raised a spiritual body. The same noun 'body' (soma) stays through every line, so this is the transformation of the body, not a swap for something non-bodily. Verse 53 says the corruptible must put on incorruption and the mortal must put on immortality, using a clothing image with the word 'it is necessary' (dei). Verse 51 says we shall all be changed at the last trumpet. Verse 54 quotes Isaiah 25:8 that death is swallowed up into victory. Philippians 3:21 says Christ will refashion the body of our lowliness so that it is conformed (symmorphon) to the body of his glory, and First John 3:2 says we shall be like him, using the adjective 'like' (homoios), because we shall see him as he is. Romans 8:18 to 23 widens the same hope to creation, which awaits the freedom of the glory of the children of God, and ties it to the redemption of the body. Two honest notes explain why readers can still differ on detail without touching the verdict. First, the words that specifically say the believer is glorified or conformed, the verb 'to glorify' (doxazo) applied to us and the rare term 'conformed' (symmorphos), are individually scarce, so the certainty comes from the whole pattern agreeing rather than from any single frequent word. Second, the timing and scheme of these events are not ranked by the vocabulary itself, which is where divergence lives. The lexical evidence is dense, repeated, and spread across several letters.
